title: Basic Accounting and Bookkeeping
tagline: From the accounting equation to final accounts, with real practice in every module
summary: Learn bookkeeping from first principles: the accounting equation, double entry, the journal and ledger, the trial balance, cash and bank, adjustments and final accounts. Every module has interactive practice and a spreadsheet lab.

modules.title: Accounting basics
modules.summary: What accounting is for, the five kinds of account and the equation that holds every set of books together.
modules.outcome: You can name the five types of account, state and apply the accounting equation and explain what each source document records.
modules.intro: Accounting is the language of business: it records what happened in money terms, so owners, lenders and tax authorities can understand it. It starts with one simple equation, and everything else is built from it.

topics.title: What accounting does
topics.html:
Bookkeeping is recording each transaction accurately. Accounting goes further: it summarises the records into reports and helps people decide. Both rest on the same principle: every transaction is recorded in money terms, on a date, with evidence.

Who uses accounts and why
UserWants to know
OwnerIs the business making a profit? Can I take money out?
BankCan this business repay a loan?
Tax authorityHow much tax is due?
SupplierWill I be paid?
InvestorIs it a good place to put money?
Tip

A rule of the trade: no evidence, no entry. Every figure in the books should trace back to a document.

Check what you just learned

1. Which user mainly asks 'can this business repay a loan?'
  • Owner
  • Employee
  • Customer
  • Bank (correct)

Lenders care about repayment ability.
keyPoints: Bookkeeping records; accounting summarises and informs.
Every entry needs evidence and a date.

topics.title: Assets, liabilities and capital: the equation
topics.html:
Formula · The accounting equation

Assets = Liabilities + Capital

What the business owns equals what it owes to outsiders plus what it owes the owner.

The five groups
GroupMeaningExamples
AssetSomething of value the business owns or is owedCash, stock, equipment, debtors
LiabilityA debt owed to outsidersBank loan, creditors
CapitalThe owner's stake: what is left after liabilitiesMoney the owner put in plus profits
IncomeMoney earnedSales, interest received
ExpenseCost of running the businessRent, wages, electricity

Predict what each transaction does

  1. Sana starts the shop with 1,00,000 rupees of her own money. Cash (an asset) and capital both rise by the same amount, so the equation stays balanced.
  2. She buys sewing machines for 30,000 paying cash. One asset goes down and another goes up: total assets are unchanged.
  3. She buys cloth worth 20,000 on credit from a supplier. Assets and liabilities both rise: she owns more and owes more.
  4. She takes a bank loan of 25,000. Cash rises and a liability rises by the same amount.
  5. She pays the supplier 10,000. Cash falls and the amount she owes falls by the same amount.

Notice that every transaction affects at least two things, and the equation stays in balance. That is the idea behind double entry, which you meet in the next module.

Check what you just learned

1. Assets are 100,000 and liabilities are 40,000. Capital is:
  • 60,000 (correct)
  • 140,000
  • 40,000
  • 100,000

Capital = Assets minus Liabilities.

2. Which is a liability?
  • Cash
  • A bank loan (correct)
  • Sales
  • Equipment

A debt owed to outsiders.
keyPoints: Assets = Liabilities + Capital, always.
Every transaction changes at least two items and keeps the equation balanced.

topics.title: Business transactions and source documents
topics.html:
Documents that start every entry
DocumentRecords
InvoiceA sale or purchase on credit
ReceiptMoney received
Cash memoA cash sale
Credit noteA refund or return
Cheque stub and bank slipPayments and deposits
Pay slipWages paid
Worked example

From document to entry

A customer pays 5,000 by cash for goods.

  1. Source document: a cash memo for 5,000.
  2. What happened: cash came in, and a sale was made.
  3. Two accounts: Cash and Sales.

Answer. Every entry begins with a document and identifies two accounts.

Common mistakes

  • Recording a transaction from memory with no document.
  • Mixing personal and business money.
  • Losing receipts: keep them filed by month.

Check what you just learned

1. A document recording a refund to a customer is:
  • An invoice
  • A pay slip
  • A credit note (correct)
  • A bank slip

Credit notes record returns and refunds.

Key terms: flip and sort

Asset
Something the business owns
Liability
A debt owed
Capital
The owner's stake
Income
Money earned
Expense
Cost of running the business
Transaction
A money event that is recorded
keyPoints: Each transaction is backed by a source document.
Keep personal and business money apart.

modules.title: Double entry and the journal
modules.summary: The rule that every transaction has a debit and a credit, and how to record transactions in the journal.
modules.outcome: You can decide which account to debit and which to credit for everyday transactions and write them up as journal entries.
modules.intro: Double entry is the heart of bookkeeping. Every transaction has two sides: something is received and something is given. We record both, so the books always balance and errors show up.

topics.title: Debit and credit
topics.html:
Definition

Debit and credit. Debit (Dr) is the left side of an account; credit (Cr) is the right. They are just left and right: neither means good or bad.

The rules: which side increases each group
Account groupIncreases with aDecreases with a
AssetDebitCredit
ExpenseDebitCredit
LiabilityCreditDebit
CapitalCreditDebit
IncomeCreditDebit

A memory aid: assets and expenses sit on the debit side of the equation, so they rise with debits. Liabilities, capital and income are on the credit side, so they rise with credits.

Worked example

Pay a rent bill

The business pays 3,000 rupees rent in cash.

  1. Rent (expense) increases, so debit Rent 3,000.
  2. Cash (asset) decreases, so credit Cash 3,000.
  3. Debits equal credits: 3,000 = 3,000.

Answer. Dr Rent 3,000; Cr Cash 3,000.

Watch out

A bank 'credit' on your statement means money came in, which is a debit in your own cash records. Statements are written from the bank's point of view.

Check what you just learned

1. Which account rises with a credit?
  • Cash
  • Equipment
  • Rent
  • Sales (correct)

Income rises with a credit.

2. Paying a supplier from cash: which account is credited?
  • Cash (correct)
  • Creditors
  • Sales
  • Rent

Cash decreases, and a decrease in an asset is a credit.
keyPoints: Debit is left, credit is right.
Assets and expenses rise with debits; liabilities, capital and income rise with credits.

topics.title: Writing journal entries
topics.html:
The journal is the book of first entry: every transaction is written here in date order, with a short narration, before it goes to the ledger. A journal entry shows the account debited, the account credited, the amounts and a note.

A journal entry
DateAccountDebitCredit
1 JanCash A/c Dr1,00,000
To Capital A/c1,00,000
(Being capital introduced by the owner)

Journalise Sana's first transactions

For each transaction choose the account to debit and the account to credit.

  1. Sana invests 1,00,000 in the business.
    Dr Cash ₹1,00,000; Cr Capital ₹1,00,000. Cash (an asset) increases, so debit it; capital increases, so credit it.
  2. She buys equipment for 30,000, paying cash.
    Dr Equipment ₹30,000; Cr Cash ₹30,000. Equipment (an asset) increases, so debit it; cash decreases, so credit it.
  3. She buys stock for 20,000 on credit.
    Dr Stock ₹20,000; Cr Creditors ₹20,000. Stock increases (debit); she owes the supplier more (credit creditors).
  4. She sells goods for 15,000 cash.
    Dr Cash ₹15,000; Cr Sales ₹15,000. Cash increases (debit); sales income increases (credit).
  5. She pays 3,000 rent.
    Dr Rent ₹3,000; Cr Cash ₹3,000. Rent is an expense, so debit it; cash decreases, so credit it.

Steps for any entry

  1. Identify the two accounts affected.
  2. Decide each account's group (asset, liability, capital, income, expense).
  3. Decide if each increases or decreases.
  4. Use the rules to decide debit or credit.
  5. Check that total debits equal total credits.

Check what you just learned

1. Buying equipment for cash: debit and credit?
  • Dr Cash, Cr Equipment
  • Dr Equipment, Cr Cash (correct)
  • Dr Capital, Cr Cash
  • Dr Rent, Cr Cash

Equipment (asset) rises, cash falls.

2. The journal is:
  • A report
  • A bank statement
  • The book of first entry (correct)
  • A tax form

Transactions enter here first.
keyPoints: The journal records every transaction first.
Total debits must equal total credits.

topics.title: Accounts and T-accounts
topics.html:
A ledger account is a page for one thing, such as Cash or Rent. A T-account draws it as a T: debits on the left, credits on the right. Over time each account collects all the entries that affect it.

A cash T-account
Debit (money in)RsCredit (money out)Rs
Capital1,00,000Equipment30,000
Sales15,000Rent3,000
Balance c/d82,000
Worked example

Reading it

The cash account above has receipts of 1,15,000 and payments of 33,000.

  1. Debit side total: 1,00,000 + 15,000 = 1,15,000.
  2. Credit side total: 30,000 + 3,000 = 33,000.
  3. Balance = 1,15,000 - 33,000 = 82,000, a debit balance (cash in hand).

Answer. A debit balance on a cash account means cash is held; a credit balance would mean an overdraft.

Tip

To find an account's balance, total each side and subtract the smaller from the larger. The larger side tells you the type of balance.

Check what you just learned

1. A cash account has debits of 50,000 and credits of 30,000. The balance is:
  • 80,000 credit
  • 0
  • 20,000 credit
  • 20,000 debit (correct)

The debit side is larger by 20,000.

Key terms: flip and sort

Debit
The left side of an account
Credit
The right side of an account
Journal
The book of first entry
Ledger
The collection of all accounts
T-account
An account drawn as a T
keyPoints: A T-account shows debits on the left and credits on the right.
The balance is the difference between the two sides.

modules.title: Ledger and trial balance
modules.summary: Post entries to the ledger, balance accounts and prove the books with a trial balance.
modules.outcome: You can post journal entries to ledger accounts, balance each account, draw up a trial balance and understand what errors it can and cannot reveal.
modules.intro: The journal records events in date order. The ledger sorts them by account, so you can see the total effect on cash, sales or rent. The trial balance then checks that the whole system is in balance.

topics.title: Posting and balancing accounts
topics.html:
To balance an account: total the debit side, total the credit side, find the difference, write it on the smaller side as 'balance carried down' (c/d), then bring it down on the other side as 'balance brought down' (b/d) to start the next period.

Worked example

Balance a cash account

Debits: 1,00,000 + 30,000 + 15,000. Credits: 40,000 + 8,000 + 12,000 + 20,000.

  1. Debit total 1,45,000; credit total 80,000.
  2. Difference 65,000, written on the credit side as balance c/d.
  3. Both sides now total 1,45,000.
  4. The balance b/d of 65,000 starts the next period on the debit side.

Answer. Cash in hand at the end of the period: 65,000.

Watch out

Never rub out an entry. If you made a mistake, correct it with a new entry that reverses it, so there is a clear record.

Check what you just learned

1. Balance c/d means:
  • Carried down (correct)
  • Brought down
  • Credit debit
  • Cancelled

It carries the balance to the next period.
keyPoints: Post each debit and credit to its own account.
Balance by totalling both sides and carrying down the difference.

topics.title: The trial balance
topics.html:
Definition

Trial balance. A list of every ledger balance, with debit balances in one column and credit balances in the other. If the books are right, the two columns have the same total.

A trial balance
AccountDebitCredit
Cash45,000
Debtors20,000
Stock30,000
Equipment60,000
Rent8,000
Salaries12,000
Creditors25,000
Capital1,00,000
Sales50,000
Totals1,75,0001,75,000

Assets and expenses have debit balances; liabilities, capital and income have credit balances. If the totals agree, the arithmetic of double entry is right.

Tip

A trial balance is a check, not a final account. It lists balances; the income statement and balance sheet come next.

Check what you just learned

1. A trial balance lists:
  • Only cash
  • All ledger balances in two columns (correct)
  • Only expenses
  • Customers

Debit and credit balances.
keyPoints: Debit balances are assets and expenses; credit balances are liabilities, capital and income.
Equal totals suggest the arithmetic is right.

topics.title: Errors a trial balance cannot find
topics.html:
If the totals disagree, an error exists. If they agree, there may still be errors that the trial balance cannot detect.

Errors and the trial balance
ErrorShows in trial balance?
A debit with no matching creditYes: totals differ
An amount added up wronglyYes: totals differ
A transaction left out entirelyNo: both sides lack it
Debit and credit both posted to the wrong accountNo: totals still agree
The wrong amount recorded on both sidesNo: totals still agree
An entry reversed (debit and credit swapped)No: totals still agree

When the totals do not agree

  1. Find the difference and check if it is a round number or half of a number.
  2. A difference divisible by 9 often points to transposed digits (e.g. 54 written as 45).
  3. Recheck additions and balances.
  4. Check that every entry was posted to both accounts.
  5. If it still cannot be found, place the difference in a suspense account until it is found.

Common mistakes

  • Forcing the trial balance to agree by adjusting a figure.
  • Assuming equal totals mean error-free books.

Check what you just learned

1. Which error will NOT show up in a trial balance?
  • A debit with no credit
  • A wrongly added balance
  • A transaction left out completely (correct)
  • A missing credit

If both sides miss it, they still agree.

Key terms: flip and sort

Posting
Copying a journal entry to the ledger
Balance c/d
Balance carried down to the next period
Trial balance
A list of balances proving debits equal credits
Suspense account
A temporary account for an unlocated difference
keyPoints: Disagreeing totals show a mistake; agreeing totals do not prove there is none.
Omissions and errors on both sides do not show in a trial balance.

modules.title: Cash and bank
modules.summary: Keep a cash book and petty cash, and reconcile your records with the bank statement.
modules.outcome: You can write up a cash book, run a petty cash system and prepare a bank reconciliation.
modules.intro: Cash is where most small businesses live and die. The cash book and the bank reconciliation are the two habits that keep it under control.

topics.title: The cash book
topics.html:
A cash book is both a journal and a ledger account for cash (and often bank). Receipts go on the debit side; payments go on the credit side. At the end of each period you total and balance it.

A simple cash book
DateReceiptRsPaymentRs
MonSales3,200Stock bought4,500
TueSales2,800Transport600
WedSales3,500Stall fee1,200
Formula · Closing cash balance

closing balance = opening balance + receipts - payments

A negative result means more has gone out than came in.

Tip

Count the actual cash at the end of each day and compare it with the book. A small difference caught today is easy to explain; a large one found next month is not.

Check what you just learned

1. Closing cash balance equals:
  • Receipts - payments
  • Payments only
  • Opening - receipts
  • Opening + receipts - payments (correct)

Start from the opening balance.
keyPoints: The cash book records receipts on the debit and payments on the credit.
Compare the book with the actual cash regularly.

topics.title: Petty cash
topics.html:
Petty cash is a small float of cash kept for minor expenses: tea, stamps, a taxi fare. The imprest system works like this: the cashier starts with a fixed float (say 5,000), pays out against signed vouchers, and at the end of the period is reimbursed exactly what was spent, bringing the float back to 5,000.

Good petty cash controls

  1. Pay out only against a signed voucher with a receipt.
  2. One person is responsible for the box.
  3. Count it regularly; cash plus vouchers must equal the float.
  4. Set a limit for a single payment.
Worked example

A petty cash check

Float 5,000. Vouchers total 3,150. Cash in the box 1,850.

  1. Vouchers + cash = 3,150 + 1,850 = 5,000.
  2. This equals the float, so the box is correct.
  3. The business reimburses 3,150 to restore the float.

Answer. Under the imprest system, cash plus vouchers always equals the float.

Check what you just learned

1. Under the imprest system, cash plus vouchers should equal:
  • The float (correct)
  • Zero
  • Sales
  • The bank balance

The float is the fixed starting amount.
keyPoints: Imprest: a fixed float, topped up to the same amount.
Cash plus vouchers must equal the float.

topics.title: Bank reconciliation
topics.html:
The bank statement and your own cash book rarely agree at any moment, mainly because of timing. A bank reconciliation explains the difference.

Why they differ
ItemCash bookBank statementEffect
Cheque issued but not yet cashed (unpresented)Already deductedNot yetStatement higher
Deposit made but not yet shown (uncredited)Already addedNot yetStatement lower
Bank charges or interestNot yet recordedAlready shownUpdate the cash book
Standing order or direct debitNot yet recordedAlready shownUpdate the cash book
Formula · Adjusted bank balance

statement balance - unpresented cheques + uncredited deposits

After these timing adjustments it should equal the cash book balance.

Worked example

Reconcile

Cash book 24,500. Statement 27,800. Unpresented cheques 4,200. Uncredited deposit 900.

  1. 27,800 - 4,200 + 900 = 24,500.
  2. That equals the cash book balance.
  3. The difference was entirely timing.

Answer. The records agree: reconciled.

Watch out

Items that appear on the statement but not in your cash book (charges, direct debits) must be entered into your cash book, because they are real.

Check what you just learned

1. A cheque you issued that the payee has not yet cashed is:
  • An uncredited deposit
  • An unpresented cheque (correct)
  • A bank charge
  • A direct debit

The bank has not yet paid it.

Key terms: flip and sort

Cash book
The record of cash and bank receipts and payments
Petty cash
A float for minor expenses
Imprest
A fixed float restored to the same amount
Unpresented cheque
Issued but not yet cashed
Reconciliation
Explaining the difference between two records
keyPoints: Unpresented cheques and uncredited deposits are timing differences.
Update the cash book for charges and direct debits.

modules.title: Adjustments and depreciation
modules.summary: Match costs to the right period with accruals, prepayments and depreciation.
modules.outcome: You can adjust for accrued and prepaid expenses and calculate straight-line depreciation and book value.
modules.intro: Cash does not always move at the moment a cost belongs to. Adjustments make sure each period carries the costs it truly used, which makes the profit figure honest.

topics.title: The matching idea: accruals and prepayments
topics.html:
Definition

Matching. Costs are recorded in the period they helped earn income, whether or not cash moved in that period.

Two kinds of adjustment
AdjustmentMeaningEffect on the expense for the year
Accrued expenseUsed or incurred, but not yet paidAdd it to the expense; it is a liability
Prepaid expensePaid in advance for a later periodRemove the part that belongs to the future; it is an asset
Worked example

Rent

Annual rent is 24,000 payable in advance. The year ends on 31 March, but the business paid 6,000 extra in advance for April to June.

  1. Cash paid this year: 30,000.
  2. Expense belonging to this year: 24,000.
  3. Prepayment (an asset): 6,000, carried forward.

Answer. Rent expense for the year is 24,000, with 6,000 shown as a prepaid asset.

Tip

Ask of each cost: which period did this benefit? Charge it there.

Check what you just learned

1. Wages earned in the last week but unpaid are:
  • Prepaid
  • Capital
  • Accrued (correct)
  • Income

They are owed at the year end.
keyPoints: Accruals add owed costs; prepayments remove costs that belong to the future.
Matching gives a truer profit.

topics.title: Depreciation
topics.html:
An asset such as a machine or van is useful for several years. Depreciation spreads its cost over those years instead of charging all of it when it is bought. It is a way of matching the cost to the years that benefit, not a cash payment.

Formula · Straight-line depreciation

yearly depreciation = (cost - scrap value) / useful life in years

The same amount every year.

A machine costing 1,20,000 with scrap value 20,000 over 5 years
YearDepreciationAccumulatedBook value
120,00020,0001,00,000
220,00040,00080,000
320,00060,00060,000
420,00080,00040,000
520,0001,00,00020,000

Change the numbers

See the yearly depreciation and the book value after any number of years.

Adjust Cost (rupees), Scrap value (rupees), Useful life (years), Years used so far and see Yearly depreciation, Book value after those years change.

Watch out

Depreciation reduces profit but does not reduce cash. The cash was spent when the asset was bought.

Check what you just learned

1. Cost 50,000, scrap 5,000, life 5 years. Yearly depreciation?
  • 45,000
  • 10,000
  • 5,000
  • 9,000 (correct)

(50,000 - 5,000) / 5 = 9,000.
keyPoints: Straight-line depreciation = (cost - scrap) / life.
Book value is cost minus accumulated depreciation.

topics.title: Bad debts and closing stock
topics.html:
A bad debt is money a customer owes but will never pay. It is an expense, and the debtor asset is reduced. A provision for doubtful debts is an estimate of bad debts to come, charged now so that profit is not overstated.

Closing stock is the goods unsold at the year end. It is not an expense of this year because it will be sold next year, so it is deducted from the cost of goods sold and shown as an asset.

Formula · Cost of goods sold

COGS = opening stock + purchases - closing stock

Only the goods actually sold in the year are charged against sales.

Worked example

The effect of stock

Opening stock 20,000. Purchases 90,000. Closing stock 30,000.

  1. COGS = 20,000 + 90,000 - 30,000 = 80,000.
  2. If you forgot closing stock, COGS would be 110,000 and profit 30,000 too low.

Answer. Forgetting closing stock understates profit; counting it twice overstates it.

Common mistakes

  • Treating unsold stock as a cost of the year.
  • Never writing off debts that will not be paid.
  • Charging a purchase of equipment all as an expense.

Check what you just learned

1. Closing stock is shown as:
  • An asset (correct)
  • An expense
  • A liability
  • Capital

It will be sold later.

Key terms: flip and sort

Accrued expense
A cost incurred but not yet paid
Prepaid expense
A cost paid in advance
Depreciation
Spreading an asset's cost over its life
Book value
Cost less accumulated depreciation
Bad debt
A debt that will not be paid
keyPoints: Bad debts are expenses; unsold stock is an asset.
COGS = opening stock + purchases - closing stock.

modules.title: Final accounts
modules.summary: Prepare an income statement and a balance sheet and read what they say.
modules.outcome: You can prepare simple final accounts from a trial balance, check that the balance sheet balances and read the key margins.
modules.intro: Final accounts are the report card of a business. The income statement shows whether it made a profit over a period; the balance sheet shows what it owns and owes at one moment.

topics.title: The income statement
topics.html:
An income statement
LineRs
Sales2,50,000
Cost of goods sold (20,000 + 1,40,000 - 30,000)1,30,000
Gross profit1,20,000
Rent24,000
Wages36,000
Depreciation10,000
Other expenses14,000
Total expenses84,000
Net profit36,000
Formula · Margins

gross margin = gross profit / sales; net margin = net profit / sales

Here: 48% and 14.4%.

Check what you just learned

1. Sales 100, COGS 60, expenses 25. Net profit?
  • 40
  • 15 (correct)
  • 25
  • 60

100 - 60 - 25 = 15.
keyPoints: Sales - COGS = gross profit; gross profit - expenses = net profit.
Margins compare profit with sales.

topics.title: The balance sheet
topics.html:
A balance sheet
AssetsRsLiabilities and capitalRs
Cash40,000Creditors25,000
Debtors25,000Bank loan20,000
Closing stock30,000Capital: opening 1,00,000
Equipment (net)60,000plus profit 18,000, less drawings 8,0001,10,000
Total1,55,000Total1,55,000
Formula · Closing capital

closing capital = opening capital + net profit - drawings

Profit increases the owner's stake; money taken out reduces it.

The two totals must agree. If they do not, an entry or a calculation is wrong. The balance sheet is a snapshot at one date, unlike the income statement, which covers a period.

Watch out

Drawings are not an expense. They are the owner taking their own money out, and they reduce capital, not profit.

Check what you just learned

1. Drawings are:
  • An expense
  • A sale
  • Money the owner takes out, reducing capital (correct)
  • An asset

They reduce the owner's stake.
keyPoints: A balance sheet lists assets against liabilities and capital at one date.
Closing capital = opening capital + profit - drawings.

topics.title: Reading the accounts
topics.html:
Quick checks
QuestionHow to check
Is it profitable?Net profit and net margin
Is the shop pricing well?Gross margin against last year or similar shops
Can it pay its short-term debts?Current assets (cash, debtors, stock) compared with creditors
Is the owner taking too much?Drawings compared with profit
Is it too reliant on borrowing?Loan compared with capital
Worked example

A quick read

Net profit 18,000 on sales of 1,50,000 with drawings of 8,000.

  1. Net margin = 12%.
  2. The owner took out 8,000 of the 18,000 profit, leaving 10,000 in the business.
  3. Capital grew from 1,00,000 to 1,10,000.

Answer. A healthy picture: profitable, with profits retained and a growing stake.

Common mistakes

  • Looking only at profit and ignoring cash.
  • Comparing margins across very different kinds of business.
  • Treating one year as a trend.
Tip

Profit is not cash. A business can be profitable on paper and still run out of money if customers pay late.

Check what you just learned

1. A business with profit but no cash is:
  • Impossible
  • A loss
  • Always safe
  • Possible if customers pay late (correct)

Timing of cash matters.

Key terms: flip and sort

Gross profit
Sales less cost of goods sold
Net profit
Gross profit less expenses
Balance sheet
Assets against liabilities and capital at one date
Drawings
Money the owner takes out
Margin
Profit as a share of sales
keyPoints: Read profit, margins, short-term strength and borrowing together.
Profit is not the same as cash.
